## In 60 seconds

Positron emission tomography (PET) and single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) image where a radioactive
tracer goes. With the glucose analog FDG, labeled with fluorine-18, PET shows metabolically active tissue,
including inflammation [@kinahan2010]. The standardized uptake value (SUV) divides the measured concentration by
the injected activity per unit body weight, after correcting that activity for decay [@kinahan2010]. Clinical PET
resolves only about 4–7 mm [@kinahan2010], so a heart wall of similar thickness reads lower than its true uptake:
the partial-volume effect [@soret2007]. In cardiac sarcoidosis with ventricular tachycardia (VT), a positive
baseline PET and a lack of improvement on repeat scans were associated with recurrence and events
[@muser2016; @muser2018]. For suspected infection of implanted devices, a multisociety consensus describes FDG
PET/CT and leukocyte SPECT/CT findings at device pockets and leads [@bourque2024].

## From the field

- **Sarcoidosis and VT ablation.** In 31 patients with cardiac sarcoidosis and VT, 23 had MRI and PET before
  ablation: late gadolinium enhancement in 21 and abnormal FDG uptake in 15. VT-free survival was 55% at two years;
  enhancement, a positive baseline PET and no improvement on repeat PET were associated with recurrence
  [@muser2016].
- **Serial quantitative PET.** In 20 patients with 92 serial scans, uptake was measured as SUVmax, a
  partial-volume-corrected SUVmean and lesion metabolic activity (corrected mean times volume). Patients whose
  lesion metabolic activity fell by less than 25% had more major cardiac events (hazard ratio 18.96, 95% CI 2.26 to
  159.27) [@muser2018], a very wide interval from few patients and events.
- **Device infection.** Consensus diagnostic features include intense FDG uptake at device pockets and leads that
  persists on images without attenuation correction [@bourque2024].
- **How reproducible is SUV?** Test-retest variability around 10% was found in carefully run studies, and more in
  practice; inconsistent uptake times were the largest single effect in one multicenter study [@kinahan2010].
- **Consensus on sarcoidosis.** An HRS expert consensus statement covers the diagnosis and management of arrhythmias
  in cardiac sarcoidosis [@birnie2014]; PubMed lists no abstract, so we cite it by title only.

## Derivations

### Decay and timing

A tracer's activity falls exponentially:

$$
A(t) = A_0\,e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}
$$ {#eq-m54-decay}

For fluorine-18, $T_{1/2}$ = 109.73 min [@tunl18f]; 68.5% remains an hour after injection (lab part A). Because SUV
uses the injected activity corrected to the scan time, an error $\Delta t$ in the recorded times scales SUV by
$2^{\Delta t/T_{1/2}}$: 6.5% for a 10-minute error, in line with the ~6% reported [@kinahan2010].

::: {.demo #m54-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m54-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m54-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m54-d2-decay.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m54-decay for fluorine-18 with the evaluated half-life [@tunl18f]; tested against `epml.nuclear`.
- Excretion and redistribution of the tracer are ignored; the curve is physical decay only. Uptake times and clock
  errors are set by the reader.
- What would change the result: a different tracer, and biological changes in uptake with time, which also change
  SUV [@kinahan2010].
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Every PET number carries a decay correction and therefore a clock.
- Consistent timing between scans matters as much as accurate timing.

### The standardized uptake value

PET measures activity concentration $C$ (kBq/mL). To compare patients and scans it is normalized:

$$
\mathrm{SUV} = \frac{C}{A'/W}
$$ {#eq-m54-suv}

where $A'$ is the net injected activity decay-corrected to the scan time and $W$ is body weight; with 1 mL of
tissue taken as 1 g, SUV is dimensionless, and a tracer spread uniformly through the body would read 1 everywhere
[@kinahan2010]. Errors in dose, residual syringe activity, weight and timing all pass straight into it (lab part B).
Blood glucose and insulin also change FDG uptake [@kinahan2010].

**Key takeaways**

- SUV is a ratio: every input has to be right.
- It normalizes dose and size, not biology.

### Partial volume in the heart wall

Model the scanner's blur as a Gaussian of full width at half maximum (FWHM) $\Gamma$, standard deviation
$\sigma = \Gamma/(2\sqrt{2\ln 2})$. A wall of thickness $w$ with uniform uptake, blurred, has the same error-function
profile as a thin wall in CT ([eq-m51-wall](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd#eq-m51-wall)). Its maximum and its mean over the true
wall recover

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{\max} = \operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{w}{2\sqrt2\,\sigma}\right), \qquad
\mathrm{RC}_{\text{mean}} = \operatorname{erf}(b) - \frac{1 - e^{-b^2}}{b\sqrt\pi}, \quad b = \frac{w}{\sqrt2\,\sigma}
$$ {#eq-m54-recovery}

of the true uptake. With clinical resolution of 4–7 mm FWHM [@kinahan2010] and an illustrative 10-mm wall, the mean
recovers 86% to 76%; at 5.5 mm, 81% (lab part C). Dividing a measured mean by $\mathrm{RC}_{\text{mean}}$ corrects it
if the geometry is known; that is the idea behind partial-volume correction, which has to contend with noise and
spill-in from neighboring tissue [@soret2007].

::: {.demo #m54-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m54-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m54-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m54-d1-partial-volume.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m54-recovery for a slab with uniform uptake in zero background and a Gaussian blur; tested against
  `epml.nuclear`.
- The blur range includes the 4–7 mm FWHM reported for clinical scanners [@kinahan2010]; wall thickness and the
  example uptake are illustrative.
- What it ignores: uptake in neighboring tissue (spill-in), cardiac and respiratory motion, noise, and the
  curvature of the real wall.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A wall as thick as the blur loses about a third of its mean uptake; one twice as thick, about a sixth.
- SUVmax recovers more than SUVmean but rests on one noisy voxel [@kinahan2010].

### Serial scans and a response rule

A response on serial PET was defined as a decrease in lesion metabolic activity of at least 25% [@muser2018]. If
each scan carries independent log-normal noise with coefficient of variation $c$, the measured ratio $R_m$ of
follow-up to baseline satisfies

$$
\ln R_m \sim \mathcal N\!\left(\ln R,\ 2\ln(1 + c^2)\right), \qquad
P(\text{called a response}) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln 0.75 - \ln R}{\sqrt{2\ln(1 + c^2)}}\right)
$$ {#eq-m54-change}

where $R$ is the true ratio and $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function. With the ~10% test-retest
variability reported for SUV [@kinahan2010], an unchanged lesion is called a response 2.1% of the time and a true 30%
decrease is missed 31% of the time (lab part E).

**Key takeaways**

- A threshold on a change inherits the noise of two scans.
- Cases near the threshold are classified partly by noise.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where nuclear imaging shows up in EP.** The cited studies use FDG PET with MRI before VT ablation in cardiac
sarcoidosis and repeat PET to follow inflammation [@muser2016; @muser2018]. An expert consensus covers arrhythmias in
cardiac sarcoidosis [@birnie2014]. For suspected infection of pacemakers, defibrillators and their leads, a
multisociety consensus describes FDG PET/CT and leukocyte SPECT/CT [@bourque2024].

**What the evidence is.** The sarcoidosis data are single-center cohorts of 20 and 31 patients
[@muser2016; @muser2018]; associations with outcome are not tests of a strategy. The device-infection guidance is
an expert consensus built with a modified Delphi process [@bourque2024].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Which number?** SUVmax, SUVmean or corrected metabolic activity behave differently (@eq-m54-recovery).
- **Were the scans comparable?** Same scanner, uptake time and preparation [@kinahan2010].
- **Is the change bigger than the noise?** Compare it with test-retest variability (@eq-m54-change).

## How experts think

Before trusting an uptake value or its change, ask:

1. **Were the times right and consistent?** Decay correction and uptake time both move SUV (see
   @eq-m54-decay and @kinahan2010).
2. **Which inputs went into SUV?** Dose, residual activity, weight, glucose (@eq-m54-suv).
3. **Is the structure thicker than the blur?** If not, the mean reads low (@eq-m54-recovery).
4. **Is the change larger than test-retest noise?** Two noisy scans make a noisier ratio (@eq-m54-change).
5. **What design produced the association?** Small cohorts give wide intervals [@muser2018].

One sentence to keep: **an uptake value is a decay-corrected, dose-normalized, blurred measurement, and its change
carries the noise of two scans.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Decay (@eq-m54-decay) | $A = A_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $\lambda = \ln2/T_{1/2}$; clock error $\Delta t$ biases SUV by $2^{\Delta t/T_{1/2}} - 1$ |
| SUV (@eq-m54-suv) | $C/(A'/W)$; uniform distribution gives 1 |
| Recovery (@eq-m54-recovery) | max $\operatorname{erf}(w/(2\sqrt2\sigma))$; mean $\operatorname{erf}(b) - (1 - e^{-b^2})/(b\sqrt\pi)$, $b = w/(\sqrt2\sigma)$ |
| Response rule (@eq-m54-change) | $P = \Phi\bigl((\ln 0.75 - \ln R)/\sqrt{2\ln(1 + c^2)}\bigr)$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Fluorine-18 half-life 109.73 min | @tunl18f |
| Clinical PET resolution 4–7 mm FWHM; test-retest ~10%; 10-min clock error ~6% | @kinahan2010 |
| Response: lesion metabolic activity decrease of at least 25% | @muser2018 |

**Studies in this module**

| Study | Question | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @muser2016 | Outcomes of VT ablation in cardiac sarcoidosis | Single-center cohort, 31 patients |
| @muser2018 | Serial quantitative FDG PET and events | Single-center cohort, 20 patients |
| @bourque2024 | Nuclear imaging for cardiovascular infection | Multisociety expert consensus |
| @birnie2014 | Arrhythmias in cardiac sarcoidosis | Expert consensus statement (cited by title) |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What does an SUV of 1 mean?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

That the tissue's concentration equals what it would be if the injected activity were spread uniformly through the
body: $C = A'/W$ (@eq-m54-suv) [@kinahan2010].

</details>

**Q2. A technician's clock is 10 minutes off. What happens to SUV?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The decay correction uses the wrong elapsed time, so SUV is off by $2^{10/109.73} - 1 \approx$ 6.5% (@eq-m54-decay),
about the 6% reported [@kinahan2010].

</details>

**Q3. Why does a normal-thickness heart wall read lower uptake than it has?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Clinical PET resolves about 4–7 mm FWHM [@kinahan2010]; a wall of comparable thickness spreads its counts into
neighbors, so its mean recovers only part of the true value (@eq-m54-recovery): about 81% for an illustrative
10-mm wall at 5.5 mm.

</details>

**Q4. SUVmax or SUVmean for follow-up?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

SUVmax is less affected by region drawing and partial volume of the mean, but it rests on one voxel and is noisier
[@kinahan2010]. Partial-volume-corrected means and metabolic activity were used in a sarcoidosis cohort
[@muser2018]. Whatever is chosen must be measured the same way each time.

</details>

**Q5. How would you correct for partial volume, and what can go wrong?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Divide by a recovery coefficient computed from the known geometry and resolution (@eq-m54-recovery), or use more
complete methods [@soret2007]. It needs the true thickness, ignores spill-in from neighbors in its simplest form, and
amplifies noise.

</details>

**Q6. A lesion's activity fell 20% on repeat PET. Did it respond?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not by a 25% rule [@muser2018], and with ~10% test-retest noise per scan [@kinahan2010] a change of that size is
within what noise alone often produces (@eq-m54-change). Check that uptake time, scanner and preparation were the
same.

</details>

**Q7. How often would noise alone call an unchanged lesion a response?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With 10% log-normal noise per scan, $\Phi(\ln 0.75/\sqrt{2\ln 1.01}) \approx$ 2% (@eq-m54-change). The bigger
problem is the other side: a true 30% fall is missed about 31% of the time.

</details>

**Q8. The hazard ratio for non-response was 18.96. How much weight does it carry?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Its 95% interval ran from 2.26 to 159.27, from 20 patients [@muser2018]: the direction is suggestive, the size is
very uncertain. It is an association in a small cohort, not an estimate to plan around.

</details>

**Q9. What do PET and SPECT measure differently?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

PET detects the two photons from positron annihilation in coincidence, which defines each line of response; SPECT
detects single photons and needs a collimator to know their direction. Both image tracer distribution; which tracer
and which scanner depend on the question, for example FDG PET or leukocyte SPECT for infection [@bourque2024].

</details>

**Q10. What does nuclear imaging add for a suspected device infection?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It can show uptake at the pocket and along leads, and extracardiac involvement; consensus features include intense
FDG uptake on device pockets and leads that persists on non-attenuation-corrected images [@bourque2024].

</details>

**Q11. Name sources of error in an SUV.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Dose and residual syringe activity, body weight, clock synchronization, uptake time, blood glucose and insulin,
scanner calibration, reconstruction and smoothing, partial volume and respiratory motion [@kinahan2010].

</details>

**Q12. Why might cardiac FDG uptake differ between two scans with no change in disease?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Different preparation (glucose and insulin), uptake time, scanner or reconstruction, and noise [@kinahan2010]; and
for thin myocardium, any change in effective resolution changes the partial-volume loss (@eq-m54-recovery).

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. What fraction of fluorine-18 remains after two half-lives?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

One quarter (@eq-m54-decay).

</details>

**S2. 350 MBq injected (decay-corrected), weight 70 kg, C = 10 kBq/mL. SUV?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$10/(350/70) = 2$ (@eq-m54-suv).

</details>

**S3. Does a heavier patient with the same dose and concentration get a higher or lower SUV?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Higher: SUV is proportional to weight at fixed $C$ and $A'$ (@eq-m54-suv).

</details>

**S4. Which recovers more of the true uptake in a thin wall, the maximum or the mean?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

The maximum (@eq-m54-recovery).

</details>

**S5. If per-scan noise doubles, what happens to the spread of the measured ratio?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

It roughly doubles too, since the log ratio's SD is $\sqrt{2\ln(1 + c^2)} \approx \sqrt2\,c$ for small
$c$ (@eq-m54-change).

</details>

**S6. True or false: a positive baseline PET caused VT recurrence in the cited cohort.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False: it was associated with recurrence in an observational cohort [@muser2016].

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Sources of SUV error.** Kinahan and Fletcher show how recovery falls for small objects, how SUV changes with
  uptake time and smoothing, and calibration drift over years [@kinahan2010;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3026294/)]. This module: the standardized uptake value
  and partial volume.
